name: Carlos Alberto Torres
milestone_by_age_26: Captained Brazil to victory in the 1970 FIFA World Cup at age 25, scoring one of the greatest goals in tournament history in the final against Italy.
early_history_summary: Carlos Alberto joined Fluminense at age 19 in 1963 and immediately stood out for his tackling, ball control, and playmaking ability as a defender. In 1966 he moved to Santos, where he became Pelé's teammate and demonstrated the leadership that led to his appointment as Brazil's national captain for the 1970 World Cup.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Brazilian football system, Santos with Pelé, Rio de Janeiro football culture, national team captaincy
evidence_summary: Carlos Alberto Torres emerged from Rio de Janeiro's football culture to join Fluminense at 19, then Santos at 22 where he played alongside Pelé. His leadership at Santos earned him the Brazil captaincy, and at 25 he captained the 1970 World Cup-winning team, scoring one of the tournament's most celebrated goals. No family background information was found in reviewed sources. His early advantages centered on immersion in Brazil's elite football ecosystem and proximity to the sport's highest level.

name: Leif Segerstam
milestone_by_age_26: Made his professional conducting debut at age 19 in 1963 with Rossini's Barber of Seville in Tampere, leading to immediate hiring by the Finnish National Opera.
early_history_summary: Born into a musical Swedish-speaking family in Vaasa, Segerstam played violin and viola in the Helsinki Youth Orchestra and studied at the Sibelius Academy from a young age, earning diplomas in violin and conducting in 1963. He then studied at the Juilliard School in New York, receiving a postgraduate diploma in 1965, and by 1968 was conducting on international tours.
family_context_summary: Born into a musical Swedish-speaking family; his father Selim Segerstam made song books for a living, creating a household immersed in music.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father Selim Segerstam was a songwriter and music book creator, providing early musical environment and domain exposure.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Sibelius Academy, Juilliard School, Finnish National Opera, musical family, Helsinki Youth Orchestra
evidence_summary: Segerstam grew up in a musical family in Finland, with his father creating song books. He studied violin and conducting at the Sibelius Academy from childhood, earning diplomas by 1963, and continued at Juilliard. His conducting debut at 19 led to a position at the Finnish National Opera, and by his mid-20s he was conducting internationally. His early advantages were rooted in Finland's elite musical institutions and his family's musical environment.

name: Stefan Edberg
milestone_by_age_26: Won his first Grand Slam singles title at the 1985 Australian Open at age 19, defeating defending champion Mats Wilander in straight sets, after achieving the junior Grand Slam in 1983.
early_history_summary: Edberg first came to attention as a junior player, winning the European Junior Championships in Under 14 and Under 16 categories, then sweeping all four junior Grand Slam titles in 1983. He turned pro in 1983, won his first singles title in Milan in 1984, and claimed his first major at the 1985 Australian Open at age 19.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Swedish tennis system, junior Grand Slam, European Junior Championships, Davis Cup team, serve-and-volley specialization
evidence_summary: Edberg rose through Sweden's tennis development system, winning European junior titles and the 1983 junior Grand Slam before turning pro. His first professional singles title came in Milan in 1984, followed by his first major at the 1985 Australian Open at age 19. No family background was documented in reviewed sources. His early advantages centered on Sweden's strong tennis ecosystem and his exceptional junior development.

name: Richard Gere
milestone_by_age_26: Fame arrived at age 28 with a supporting role in Looking for Mr. Goodbar (1977) and age 31 with American Gigolo (1980); by 26 he had only minor stage work including a Broadway flop and a London production of Grease, with no material milestone found.

name: Stephen Hawking
milestone_by_age_26: Completed his PhD at Cambridge in 1966 with a groundbreaking thesis on singularities in cosmology, received the Adams Prize the same year, and published multiple papers in the Proceedings of the Royal Society by age 24-26.
early_history_summary: Hawking began his physics degree at Oxford at age 17, earning a first-class BA. He moved to Cambridge for graduate work under Dennis Sciama in 1962, was diagnosed with motor neurone disease in 1963 at age 21, and completed his PhD in 1966 with a thesis on properties of expanding universes that laid the groundwork for the Penrose-Hawking singularity theorems.
family_context_summary: Born in Oxford into a family of physicians; his father Frank was a medical researcher specializing in tropical diseases and both parents attended the University of Oxford, though the family faced financial constraints.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a medical researcher at Oxford; Hawking said he modelled himself on his father and viewed scientific research as the natural path, providing early domain exposure to scientific thinking.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Oxford, Cambridge, Dennis Sciama, Roger Penrose, Adams Prize, ALS diagnosis as catalyst, family of physicians
evidence_summary: Hawking grew up in an academic family in Oxford, with his father a medical researcher who modelled the scientific path. He attended Oxford and Cambridge, studying under Dennis Sciama and collaborating with Roger Penrose on singularity theorems. His 1966 PhD thesis and Adams Prize established him as a significant physicist by age 24. His ALS diagnosis at 21 created extraordinary urgency that catalyzed his focus. His early advantages centered on elite institutional access and family scientific culture, compounded by the adversity of his diagnosis.

name: John Sulston
milestone_by_age_26: Completed PhD in 1966 at age 24 and worked as a postdoctoral researcher at the Salk Institute through 1969; Nobel-winning C. elegans cell lineage work began in 1974 at age 32. No material milestone by 26 found beyond standard academic progression.

name: Mario J. Molina
milestone_by_age_26: Earned BS from UNAM (1965) and MS from University of Freiburg (1967), briefly served as associate professor at UNAM (1967-68), and enrolled in PhD program at UC Berkeley in 1968; Nobel-winning CFC-ozone depletion research was published in 1974 at age 31. No material milestone by 26 found beyond standard academic progression.

name: Mikhail Baryshnikov
milestone_by_age_26: Won gold medal at the Varna International Ballet Competition in 1966 at age 18, joined the Kirov Ballet as a soloist in 1967 bypassing the corps entirely, and won gold at the Moscow International Ballet Competition and the Nijinsky Prize in 1969.
early_history_summary: Baryshnikov began ballet studies in Riga at age 12 in 1960. In 1964 he entered the Vaganova School in Leningrad under Alexander Pushkin, won the Varna junior division in 1966, and joined the Kirov Ballet in 1967 as a soloist. Soviet choreographers created roles specifically for him, and by 1969 he had won the Moscow Competition and Nijinsky Prize.
family_context_summary: Born into a Russian family in Riga, Latvia; his father was a Soviet colonel with whom he had a difficult relationship, and his mother committed suicide during his early teens, after which he began studying ballet seriously.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a Soviet military colonel, not connected to dance; no family domain advantage in ballet documented.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Vaganova School, Kirov Ballet, Alexander Pushkin, Varna gold medal, Soviet ballet system, skipped corps de ballet, mother's suicide
evidence_summary: Baryshnikov began ballet at 12 in Riga after his mother's suicide, then entered the elite Vaganova School under Alexander Pushkin. His exceptional talent led to a Varna gold medal at 18, direct soloist status at the Kirov Ballet at 19, and multiple international competition wins by 21. NYT critic Clive Barnes called him 'the most perfect dancer I have ever seen' while still in the USSR. His early advantages were dominated by the Soviet ballet pipeline and an extraordinary physical edge recognized early.

name: Riccardo Muti
milestone_by_age_26: Won the prestigious Guido Cantelli Conducting Competition by unanimous jury vote in Milan in 1967 at age 26, becoming the first Italian to win the prize and leading to his appointment as principal conductor of the Maggio Musicale Fiorentino in 1968.
early_history_summary: Muti studied piano at the Conservatory of San Pietro a Majella in Naples under Vincenzo Vitale, then earned diplomas in composition and conducting at the Giuseppe Verdi Conservatory in Milan under Bruno Bettinelli and Antonino Votto, also studying with Nino Rota. His unanimous Cantelli Prize win in 1967 launched his international career.
family_context_summary: Born in Naples, spent early childhood in Molfetta, Apulia. Father Domenico was a pathologist and amateur singer with a great love of music; mother Gilda was a reserved Neapolitan woman. Middle-class family with five children.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a pathologist who was also an amateur singer and great music lover, creating a musically rich household environment that complemented Muti's conservatory training.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Conservatory of San Pietro a Majella, Giuseppe Verdi Conservatory Milan, Nino Rota, Antonino Votto, Cantelli Prize, Italian operatic tradition, father's musical influence
evidence_summary: Muti grew up in a household where his father, a pathologist, was an amateur singer and passionate music lover. He trained at elite Italian conservatories in Naples and Milan, studying with notable teachers including Nino Rota and Antonino Votto. His unanimous win of the Cantelli Prize at 26 launched his career, leading to the Maggio Musicale Fiorentino position. His early advantages centered on Italy's elite conservatory pipeline and his father's musical influence.

name: André the Giant
milestone_by_age_26: Professional wrestling debut in 1966 at age 19, toured internationally through France, UK, Japan, and Canada by his mid-20s, but major fame as WWWF special attraction began in 1973 at age 27; WrestleMania and WWF Championship came in the 1980s. No material milestone by 26 found.

name: Giuseppe Sinopoli
milestone_by_age_26: Appointed professor of contemporary and electronic music at the Benedetto Marcello Conservatory in Venice in 1972 at age 26, with compositions performed at major venues including Teatro La Fenice in 1971, while simultaneously holding a medical doctorate.
early_history_summary: Sinopoli studied harmony and organ from age 12, then at the Venice Conservatory under Ernesto Rubin de Cervin, while simultaneously pursuing medicine at the University of Padua. He studied composition at Darmstadt under Stockhausen and at the Accademia Chigiana under Donatoni, and began conducting studies with Hans Swarowsky in Vienna, founding the Bruno Maderna Ensemble in the early 1970s.
family_context_summary: Father insisted on medical studies alongside music, leading Sinopoli to obtain a doctorate in medicine with emphasis on psychiatry from the University of Padua while pursuing composition. Family financial background not documented in reviewed sources.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was not in music but insisted on medical studies, creating a dual-track constraint; no family domain advantage in music documented.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Venice Conservatory, Darmstadt, Stockhausen, Donatoni, Swarowsky, Bruno Maderna Ensemble, dual medicine-music path, Teatro La Fenice
evidence_summary: Sinopoli pursued music and medicine simultaneously, studying composition at Venice Conservatory, Darmstadt under Stockhausen, and conducting in Vienna under Swarowsky. By 26 he was a professor at the Venice Conservatory with compositions performed at Teatro La Fenice. His father's insistence on medical studies created a constraint that he navigated while building his musical career. His early advantages centered on elite European musical institutions and mentorship from leading avant-garde composers.

name: Felice Gimondi
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 1965 Tour de France at age 22 in his first year as a professional cyclist, becoming one of the youngest Tour winners in history, and won the Giro d'Italia in 1967 at age 25.
early_history_summary: Gimondi grew up in Sedrina, Bergamo, the son of a transport manager and a post mistress. He frequently used his mother's post bicycle as a youth and began amateur racing in 1963, winning the Tour de l'Avenir in 1964. He turned professional with Salvarani in 1965 and, as a last-minute replacement, won the Tour de France in his debut professional season.
family_context_summary: Son of a transport manager and a post mistress in Sedrina, Bergamo. Working-class background; he had to ask his mother's permission to start the 1965 Tour de France as a last-minute replacement.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents were not in cycling; father was a transport manager, mother was a post mistress. No family domain advantage in cycling documented.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Italian cycling culture, Salvarani team, Tour de l'Avenir, last-minute Tour replacement, working-class background, post bicycle, Bergamo
evidence_summary: Gimondi came from a working-class family in Bergamo, Italy, and began competitive cycling relatively late at age 21. He won the Tour de l'Avenir in 1964 and, after turning professional with Salvarani, won the 1965 Tour de France as a last-minute replacement in his first pro season at age 22. His early advantages were modest—primarily Italy's cycling culture and the Salvarani team—while his breakthrough was driven by exceptional physical talent and opportunity seized under constraint.
